catalog_quote: [3.5] There are no second-position clitics of the Wackernagel type. The extent to which we should recognize phonological clitics is debatable. There are many function elements, often monosyllabic or subsyllabic, that could be considered as affixes, clitics, or particles (or, in verb complexes, auxiliaries). ... There is no stress or accent system that would clearly distinguish affixes, clitics, and particles. ... [3.6] Individual syllables are usually L or H, but contour-toned syllables <HL> and <LH> also occur in monosyllabics and in word-final syllables. <LHL> is rare ... There are no <HLH> syllables. ... [3.6.1.1] In nouns and numerals, and to a lesser extent adjectives, stems have a lexical tone melody. Tiranige belongs to the subset of Dogon languages that allow lexically /L/-toned stems. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Tiranige has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so nothing to agree or disagree with; this work supplies the first statement: tonal language with lexical tone melodies, and per the author no stress/accent system. Compatible with the empty catalog entry and adds the type.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tiranige is described as a tone language (lexical tone melodies /H/, /HL/, /LH/, /L/, rarely /LHL/, /HLH/ on nouns and numerals; verb and adjective tones assigned by the grammar; tonosyntactic overlays). The only statement about stress is a negative one: Heath says there is no stress or accent system (phrased as none that would clearly diagnose affix vs clitic vs particle status). The grammar does recognise a metrical weak position (the medial syllable of CvCvCv), which conditions vowel raising and syncope, but this is not presented as stress; no syllable is described as stressed anywhere in the 330 pages (single hit each for 'stress' and 'accent', zero for 'prominence').
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The statement is hedged as a diagnostic claim ('that would clearly distinguish affixes, clitics, and particles') rather than a flat typological one, but no positive stress facts are given anywhere in the work. Intonational pitch rise/drop (§3.8) and intonational prolongation are described as phrase-level intonation, not word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2020 Zenodo PDF is Heath's draft dated February 2017 (title page: 'draft dated February 2017, based on brief fieldwork, do not quote without permission'). Data come from two speakers: a young assistant from Boui (plains; most elicited examples) and an older shopkeeper of the cordonnier caste from Ningo (2013 texts); Heath notes 'considerable differences' between the Boui and Ningo dialects (e.g. intervocalic *b > w in Boui only) but the stress statement is made for the language as a whole. The later 2022 version of the same grammar (Zenodo 6350672, 444 pp., downloaded for comparison only, same overflow dir) repeats the sentence verbatim on p. 33.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2014. Replacive grammatical tone in the Dogon languages. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles. Open copies:https://escholarship.org/uc/item/7hh0k529;https://linguistics.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/McPherson_dissertation.pdf
tone_statements.quote: There are two phonemic tones, H and L, marked with acute (v́) and grave (v̀) accents, respectively; unmarked syllables are toneless. … The pattern we ﬁnd in Tiranige is as follows: the ﬂoating tone is realized as L after a H-toned word and as H after a L-toned word (tone polarity); in each case, the ﬂoating tone docks to the right edge, replacing the tone of the ﬁnal syllable. … Cases where the ﬂoating tone is not realized include monosyllabic H-toned nouns and bitonal words (/LH/, /HL/).
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, H and L; a word's lexical tones are replaced by grammatical overlays {L}, {LH}, {H} conditioned by adjacent words in the noun phrase; definite ri carries a floating H showing tone polarity.

tone_statements.quote: p. 29 (§3.5): "There is no stress or accent system that would clearly distinguish affixes, clitics, and particles." p. 30 (§3.6.1.1): "In nouns and numerals, and to a lesser extent adjectives, stems have a lexical tone melody. [...] Tiranige belongs to the subset of Dogon languages that allow lexically /L/-toned stems, so there is no requirement that all stems have at least one H-tone." p. 30 (§3.6.1.2): "Verbs have no lexical tones, and there are no \"bare\" verb stems. [...] The tones of the stem depend on the inflectional category." p. 32 (§3.6.1.3): "In sum, the basic lexical tone classes for nouns are /H/, /HL/, /LH/, and /L/, while /LHL/ and /HLH/ are very rare. The lexical melody is audible where there is no following adjective or determiner, and there is no preceding possessor. The basic possessor-controlled tone contour is {LH}"

audit.reasoning: The 'tonal' (no stress/accent system) coding rests on the sole and current reference grammar (Heath 2022, 444 pp.), which we hold; the deciding sentence and the supporting tone and metrical-structure passages are verbatim at the stated pages (p. 33/PDF 48, p. 34/PDF 49, p. 15/PDF 30). Heath explicitly says there is no stress or accent system and describes syllable-level H/L/contour tones with lexical melodies and grammatical overlays; the only 'metrical' remark (weak medial syllable in CvCvCv conditioning raising/syncope) is already captured in the record's the secondary-stress rule and does not amount to a stress rule. Glottolog lists no other descriptive works and Zenodo shows no newer version or separate phonology study, so nothing available would change the classification. No works still to obtain.

sources.note: Mentioned in passing in a cross-Dogon study: L vs H tone as in all Dogon languages; a possessor imposes an {LH} overlay on the noun (gàànà 'cat', X gààná 'X's cat'). No Tiranige tone sketch here.

tone.quote: Like all Dogon languages, it has a phonemic distinction between L and H tone … If we bring western Dogon languages such as Bunoge (Heath 2012a) and Tiranige (Heath 2012b) into the picture, we can also cite {LH} overlays on nouns. {LH} can be required by controllers either to the right (adjectives) as in Bunoge sùgùlè ‘ear’ but modified sùgùléLH bı̀gı̀ ‘big ear’, or to the left (possessors) as in Tiranige gàànà ‘cat’ but possessed X LH gààná ‘X’s cat’. A {LH} melody is incompatible with a reduction/culminativity model since the overlay can actually introduce H tones

sources.note: Dogon NP tonosyntax arose from (a) a right-headed prosodic pattern in noun-modifier sequences, (b) loss of numeral classifiers that had protected nouns from that pattern before numerals, and (c) transfer of tones from possessors to following possessums; the resulting system was reinterpreted semantically and is stable. Bears on the origin of the possessor/modifier tone overlays described for Tiranige.

sources.note: Dogon DP tonosyntax can often be reduced to schemata [T O C] or [C O T] in which a reference-restricting controller imposes a tonal overlay on an adjacent target word or string; with two or more controllers the outermost usually controls the whole inner string (Poss-N-Adj-Num realized as [Poss O[N Adj Num]]); but several Dogon languages have DP tone patterns that no combination of binary schemata generates, calling for a noncompositional constructional tonosyntactic model, with numerals catalysing latent tonal control by definites and postposed possessors.
